title: Physical Chemistry III
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Physical Chemistry III curriculum: quantum chemistry and atomic structure, chemical bonding theories (VBT/MOT), molecular symmetry, photochemistry, and surface chemistry/catalysis. Chemical kinetics and spectroscopy are treated as dedicated courses elsewhere (CHM402, CHM410) so are only touched lightly here.

questions.question: De Broglie's hypothesis proposes that a particle of momentum p has an associated wavelength given by:
options: λ = h/p
λ = p/h
λ = hp
λ = h²/p
questions.correct_answer: λ = h/p
questions.explanation: De Broglie's relation λ = h/p (h = Planck's constant) assigns a wave character to moving particles, unifying wave and particle descriptions of matter.

questions.question: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle states that:
options: Energy of an electron in an atom is always quantized
It is impossible to simultaneously know the exact position and exact momentum of a particle
Electrons always occupy the lowest available energy orbital
No two electrons in an atom can have identical quantum numbers
questions.correct_answer: It is impossible to simultaneously know the exact position and exact momentum of a particle
questions.explanation: The uncertainty principle sets a fundamental limit: Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π, so position and momentum cannot both be known with arbitrary precision.

questions.question: The Schrödinger wave equation, when solved for a given system, yields:
options: The exact trajectory of an electron
Wavefunctions (ψ) and corresponding allowed energy values
Only the mass of the particle
The rate constant of a chemical reaction
questions.correct_answer: Wavefunctions (ψ) and corresponding allowed energy values
questions.explanation: Solving the Schrödinger equation for a system gives permissible wavefunctions and their associated quantized energies; ψ² gives the probability density of finding the particle.

questions.question: The principal quantum number (n) of an atomic orbital primarily determines:
options: The shape of the orbital
The orientation of the orbital in space
The overall size and energy of the orbital
The spin of the electron
questions.correct_answer: The overall size and energy of the orbital
questions.explanation: n specifies the shell (energy level); larger n means a larger, higher-energy orbital.

questions.question: The azimuthal (angular momentum) quantum number, l, determines:
options: The shape of the subshell/orbital
The exact energy of a multi-electron atom's orbital only
The spin direction of the electron
The number of protons in the nucleus
questions.correct_answer: The shape of the subshell/orbital
questions.explanation: l defines the orbital's angular momentum and hence its shape (l = 0, 1, 2, 3 correspond to s, p, d, f subshells).

questions.question: According to the Pauli exclusion principle:
options: Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly before pairing
No two electrons in the same atom can have an identical set of all four quantum numbers
Every orbital can hold a maximum of one electron
Electrons occupy the highest energy orbital available
questions.correct_answer: No two electrons in the same atom can have an identical set of all four quantum numbers
questions.explanation: The Pauli exclusion principle limits each orbital to at most two electrons, which must have opposite spins.

questions.question: Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity states that:
options: Electrons pair up in an orbital before occupying a new one of equal energy
Degenerate orbitals are singly occupied with parallel spins before any pairing occurs
Lower energy orbitals are always filled last
Electron spin has no effect on orbital filling order
questions.correct_answer: Degenerate orbitals are singly occupied with parallel spins before any pairing occurs
questions.explanation: Hund's rule minimises electron-electron repulsion by spreading electrons singly across degenerate orbitals with parallel spin before pairing begins.

questions.question: Einstein's explanation of the photoelectric effect established that:
options: Light behaves purely as a continuous wave with no particle character
Electrons are ejected only if the frequency of incident light exceeds a threshold value, regardless of intensity
Increasing light intensity alone can eject electrons at any frequency
The kinetic energy of ejected electrons depends only on the light's intensity
questions.correct_answer: Electrons are ejected only if the frequency of incident light exceeds a threshold value, regardless of intensity
questions.explanation: Einstein showed light is quantized into photons of energy hf; electron ejection requires hf to exceed the metal's work function, independent of intensity.

questions.question: A photon has a wavelength of 400 nm. Using E = hc/λ (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s), its energy is approximately:
In molecular orbital theory, a bonding molecular orbital is:
options: Higher in energy than the atomic orbitals that formed it
Lower in energy than the atomic orbitals that formed it, increasing electron density between nuclei
Always empty in a stable molecule
Formed only from destructive overlap of atomic orbitals
questions.correct_answer: Lower in energy than the atomic orbitals that formed it, increasing electron density between nuclei
questions.explanation: Constructive overlap of atomic orbitals produces a bonding MO of lower energy, stabilising the molecule by concentrating electron density between the nuclei.

questions.question: Using molecular orbital theory, the bond order of the O2 molecule is:
questions.explanation: O2's MO configuration gives 8 bonding and 4 antibonding valence electrons; bond order = (8−4)/2 = 2.

questions.question: Molecular orbital theory correctly predicts a property of O2 that valence bond theory fails to explain, namely that O2 is:
options: Colourless
Paramagnetic, due to two unpaired electrons in π* antibonding orbitals
Diamagnetic
Non-polar
questions.correct_answer: Paramagnetic, due to two unpaired electrons in π* antibonding orbitals
questions.explanation: MOT places two electrons singly in degenerate π*2p orbitals, correctly predicting O2's observed paramagnetism, which simple Lewis/VBT structures miss.

questions.question: A sigma (σ) bond, compared to a pi (π) bond, is best described as:
options: Formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals and weaker
Formed by head-on (axial) overlap of orbitals and generally stronger, with free rotation possible about it
Always formed only between two s orbitals
Present only in ionic compounds
questions.correct_answer: Formed by head-on (axial) overlap of orbitals and generally stronger, with free rotation possible about it
questions.explanation: σ bonds arise from direct end-on orbital overlap along the internuclear axis, giving a stronger bond that permits free rotation, unlike the sideways-overlapping π bond.

questions.question: The central carbon atom in methane (CH4) is best described, using valence bond theory, as:
options: sp hybridised, linear
sp² hybridised, trigonal planar
sp³ hybridised, tetrahedral
sp³d hybridised, trigonal bipyramidal
questions.correct_answer: sp³ hybridised, tetrahedral
questions.explanation: Carbon in methane forms four equivalent σ bonds using four sp³ hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedrally (bond angle ~109.5°).

questions.question: By VSEPR theory, the molecular geometry of ammonia (NH3), which has one lone pair on nitrogen, is:
options: Trigonal planar
Tetrahedral
Trigonal pyramidal
Linear
questions.correct_answer: Trigonal pyramidal
questions.explanation: Nitrogen has four electron domains (3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pair) arranged tetrahedrally, but the molecular shape (ignoring the lone pair) is trigonal pyramidal.

questions.question: In molecular symmetry, a C2 rotation axis is a symmetry element about which rotation by:
options: 360° restores the original molecule and no other angle does
180° restores the molecule to an indistinguishable orientation
90° restores the molecule
60° restores the molecule
questions.correct_answer: 180° restores the molecule to an indistinguishable orientation
questions.explanation: A Cn axis corresponds to rotation by 360°/n giving an equivalent configuration; for C2, that angle is 180°.

questions.question: The point group of a water molecule (bent, with two mirror planes and a C2 axis) is:
options: C2v
D2h
Td
C3v
questions.correct_answer: C2v
questions.explanation: Water has a C2 principal axis and two vertical mirror planes (σv), placing it in the C2v point group.

questions.question: The Grotthuss–Draper law of photochemistry states that:
options: Every photon absorbed activates exactly two molecules
Only light that is absorbed by a system can bring about a photochemical change in it
Photochemical reactions can occur without light absorption
The quantum yield of every reaction must equal 1
questions.correct_answer: Only light that is absorbed by a system can bring about a photochemical change in it
questions.explanation: This first law of photochemistry establishes that unabsorbed light (reflected or transmitted) has no photochemical effect.

questions.question: The Stark–Einstein law of photochemical equivalence states that:
options: Each molecule taking part in a photochemical reaction absorbs one photon (quantum) of the radiation causing the reaction
The energy of a photon is independent of its frequency
All absorbed photons must produce a reaction
Quantum yield can never exceed 0.5
questions.correct_answer: Each molecule taking part in a photochemical reaction absorbs one photon (quantum) of the radiation causing the reaction
questions.explanation: This second law of photochemistry states the primary photochemical act involves absorption of one photon per activated molecule.

questions.question: Quantum yield (Φ) in photochemistry is defined as:
options: The number of photons absorbed divided by the number of molecules reacted
The number of molecules reacted (or product formed) divided by the number of photons absorbed
The total energy of light absorbed
The rate constant of the photochemical reaction
questions.correct_answer: The number of molecules reacted (or product formed) divided by the number of photons absorbed
questions.explanation: Φ = (molecules reacted)/(photons absorbed); chain reactions can give Φ >> 1, while inefficient processes give Φ < 1.

questions.question: The key distinction between fluorescence and phosphorescence is that:
options: Fluorescence involves emission from a triplet state and persists after the light source is removed
Phosphorescence is emission from an excited singlet state and stops immediately when excitation ends
Fluorescence is a rapid singlet-to-singlet emission that stops almost immediately when excitation ends, while phosphorescence involves a triplet state and can persist afterward
There is no fundamental difference between the two phenomena
questions.correct_answer: Fluorescence is a rapid singlet-to-singlet emission that stops almost immediately when excitation ends, while phosphorescence involves a triplet state and can persist afterward
questions.explanation: Fluorescence is a spin-allowed S1→S0 transition (fast, ~ns), while phosphorescence requires intersystem crossing to a triplet state, making the spin-forbidden T1→S0 emission much slower and longer-lived.

questions.question: Adsorption in surface chemistry is best defined as:
options: The uniform distribution of a substance throughout the bulk of another
The accumulation of a substance at the surface or interface of two phases
The dissolution of a gas completely into a liquid
A change of state from liquid to gas
questions.correct_answer: The accumulation of a substance at the surface or interface of two phases
questions.explanation: Adsorption is a surface phenomenon where adsorbate molecules concentrate at the surface of an adsorbent, distinct from absorption which is a bulk phenomenon.

questions.question: Compared with physisorption, chemisorption is characterised by:
options: Weak van der Waals forces, low heat of adsorption, and easy reversibility
Formation of chemical bonds, higher heat of adsorption, and being largely irreversible and specific
No dependence on temperature at all
Occurring only above the boiling point of the adsorbate
questions.correct_answer: Formation of chemical bonds, higher heat of adsorption, and being largely irreversible and specific
questions.explanation: Chemisorption involves actual chemical bond formation between adsorbate and adsorbent, giving much higher adsorption enthalpies (40-400 kJ/mol) than physisorption and strong specificity.

questions.question: The Langmuir adsorption isotherm is derived assuming:
options: Multilayer adsorption with unlimited adsorption sites
Adsorption occurs as a monolayer on identical, energetically equivalent sites with no interaction between adsorbed molecules
Adsorption is independent of pressure/concentration
The adsorbent surface is heterogeneous with sites of widely varying energy
questions.correct_answer: Adsorption occurs as a monolayer on identical, energetically equivalent sites with no interaction between adsorbed molecules
questions.explanation: Langmuir's model assumes a fixed number of equivalent surface sites, monolayer coverage, and no lateral interaction between adsorbed species.

questions.question: The Freundlich adsorption isotherm is an empirical relationship of the form x/m = kP^(1/n), which, unlike the Langmuir isotherm:
options: Assumes a perfectly homogeneous surface with a saturation limit
Does not predict a true saturation (maximum adsorption) limit and fits heterogeneous surfaces better at intermediate pressures
Applies only to chemisorption
Requires no experimental constants
questions.correct_answer: Does not predict a true saturation (maximum adsorption) limit and fits heterogeneous surfaces better at intermediate pressures
questions.explanation: The Freundlich isotherm is purely empirical, with constants k and n fitted from data, and does not level off to a fixed saturation value the way the Langmuir isotherm does.

questions.question: In heterogeneous catalysis, the general mechanism proceeds through the sequence:
options: Desorption, then reaction, then adsorption
Adsorption of reactants onto the catalyst surface, surface reaction, then desorption of products
The catalyst is consumed permanently in the first step
Reaction occurs entirely in the gas phase away from the catalyst surface
questions.correct_answer: Adsorption of reactants onto the catalyst surface, surface reaction, then desorption of products
questions.explanation: Heterogeneous catalysis lowers activation energy by first adsorbing reactants onto active sites, allowing reaction to occur on the surface before products desorb, regenerating the catalyst.

questions.question: The BET (Brunauer–Emmett–Teller) theory extends the Langmuir model primarily to:
options: Describe chemisorption kinetics
Account for multilayer physical adsorption, enabling determination of a solid's surface area
Explain colligative properties of solutions
Predict reaction rate constants
questions.correct_answer: Account for multilayer physical adsorption, enabling determination of a solid's surface area
questions.explanation: BET theory generalises Langmuir's monolayer treatment to multilayer physisorption, and BET plots are the standard method for measuring specific surface area of porous solids.

questions.question: According to the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, as temperature increases, the fraction of molecules possessing energy greater than a fixed activation energy Ea:
options: Decreases
Increases
Remains exactly constant
Becomes zero
questions.correct_answer: Increases
questions.explanation: Raising temperature broadens and shifts the Maxwell–Boltzmann energy distribution, increasing the fraction of molecules with energy above any fixed threshold, which is why reaction rates rise with temperature.

questions.question: A colloidal catalyst such as finely divided platinum is effective mainly because:
options: It increases the surface area available for adsorption of reactants, providing more active sites
It changes the thermodynamic equilibrium position of the reaction
It permanently reacts with and is consumed by the reactant
It lowers the temperature of the reaction mixture
questions.correct_answer: It increases the surface area available for adsorption of reactants, providing more active sites
questions.explanation: Finely divided catalysts expose a much larger surface area per unit mass, increasing the number of active adsorption sites and hence the catalytic rate, without shifting the equilibrium.

questions.question: In an octahedral field for a d-orbital set (relevant to bonding of transition-metal-containing systems), the electron configuration term used to describe the ground electronic state of a molecule is called a:
options: Rate law
Term symbol
Rydberg constant
Partition function
questions.correct_answer: Term symbol
questions.explanation: A term symbol summarises the total orbital and spin angular momentum of an electronic state, a concept from atomic/quantum theory used to classify electronic states.

questions.question: The energy levels of a particle confined in a one-dimensional 'particle in a box' model are:
options: Continuous, with all energies allowed
Quantized, proportional to n², where n is a positive integer quantum number
Independent of the box length
Always equal to zero
questions.correct_answer: Quantized, proportional to n², where n is a positive integer quantum number
questions.explanation: Solving the Schrödinger equation for a particle in a box gives En = n²h²/8mL², showing quantized energies that increase with the square of the quantum number n.
